body: Simulated students let researchers test tutoring systems and teaching strategies before real learners are available, but only if the simulation reproduces where a particular learner succeeds and fails. The common approach asks a large language model to role-play a student, but a role does not model what this learner knows or will do next, so the model's own competence fills the gap. Simulated students perform at a level set by the model, differ little from one another, and seldom make the real learners' errors. We model the learner's behavior and recast student simulation as third-person prediction of the learner's next action. HACHIMI-II builds a student model from the learner's history, infers the learner's state for the current item or tutor turn, and compiles it into a behavior harness that constrains the next action. On three item-response datasets, the Wasserstein-1 distance between simulated and real student ability is 2.4--8.4× smaller than that of the strongest baseline. On two dialogue datasets, HACHIMI-II reproduces real student errors with the same knowledge type, locus, and mechanism 1.8--5.1× more often than the strongest baseline, and ablations trace the gains mainly to the explicit learner state. Predicting the learner makes capable models usable as simulated students.
summaryZh: HACHIMI-II：从角色扮演到忠实学生模拟的学习者行为建模。模拟学生让研究人员在真正的学习者可用之前测试辅导系统和教学策略，但前提是模拟重现特定学习者成功和失败的情况。常见的方法要求大型语言模型对学生进行角色扮演，但角色并不能模拟学习者知道的内容或下一步将要做什么，因此模型自身的能力填补了空白。
